risk.line: Moscow shut the door it had cracked open twenty-four hours earlier - Peskov declared the peace track on a "deep pause" with "no new proposals whatsoever" while Russian troops press Pokrovsk and Kupiansk. On the other file Iran's foreign minister called diplomacy "not impossible" on the same day the US Treasury secretary promised to crush Iran's economy at the G20. Two capitals talked past two counterparts, and the strait's traffic ticked back down.

hypotheses.name: IRGC captured the succession (weak form — assessed finding)
hypotheses.d: Documented pressure on Assembly electors, 8 boycotts, overridden shortlist and will. The pre-arranged-pact version scores only 30% — the plan was overridden, not executed.

hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — 75% → 82%
hypotheses.d: Week's biggest mover, on three strands independent of the Israeli/exile channel. Pezeshkian said on Iranian state TV that communication with Khamenei is 'very difficult' — Tehran's own president, against his own interest. Washington routed its peace offer not to Araghchi but to Mohsen Rezaee, career IRGC commander-in-chief now running the security council. Cipher Brief: 'Tehran isn't saying who is actually in charge.' Capped at 82% because the state has promised footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders — that is the falsifier, and it is coming.

hypotheses.name: Nobody’s hurrying on Hormuz — HELD at 60%
hypotheses.d: The near-breakthrough-then-condition pattern fired a sixth time (Iran–Oman interim corridor and 30–60 days of technical talks, against Ghalibaf restating the full condition stack). Deliberately not moved: it is already priced, and a minesweeping calendar is what an honest process looks like too. The real test is live — the offer sits with the IRGC, so Tehran's answer is the experiment.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — 55% → 60%
hypotheses.d: The discriminating split signal arrived: PLA sorties kept declining while the coast guard escalated in kind — CCG 2307 pressing a Japanese coast guard ship in the strait Aug 6–10, which AEI reads as testing whether foreign vessels will obey PRC authority. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up is the ratchet signature. Capped at +5; the stated tell is what the coast guard does through the Sept 24 visit.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — 45% → 52%
hypotheses.d: Economic Outcast hit ~60 teapots, tankers and traders and touched no Chinese state major and no bank — Treasury sent the majors a warning letter instead. Maximum pressure on Iran, calibrated to stop exactly short of anything that would detonate the Sept 24 summit. Held to +7 because the Munir offer is a real concession, and $4.10 gas before midterms is real evidence against premeditation.

hypotheses.name: NEW · A pre-announcement leak into oil futures
hypotheses.d: Four times in the war window, nine- and ten-figure short bets landed 15–20 minutes before an Iran announcement: ~$2.2bn across crude, gasoil and gasoline before Trump's Mar 23 pause post; ~$950m before the Apr 7 ceasefire; ~$760m before Iran said Hormuz would open. ~$7bn total; CFTC probing, four members of Congress demanding answers. Split: deliberate leak 45 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 25 / coincidence 10. This is the only entry in the book whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event rather than pattern-matched after — which is why it opens this high. Against it: no episode has surfaced around this week's diplomacy.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 30% → 25%
hypotheses.d: Cut again. The channels that actually moved this week were Oman, Pakistan and the new Mecca defence pact — Russia was absent from every one of them, and still has not offered the mediation this hypothesis expects. Motive 9/10, documentary evidence 0/10, pre-event evidence never. Cut to 15% if nothing surfaces by Sept 30.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Both its live predictions came in favourably this week and it gets credit for neither: the rival leverage hypothesis predicted the same things, and shared predictions are ambience. One more failed pre-summit call and it goes to the epitaph list.

brief.h: Moscow closes the window it opened yesterday
brief.t: Dmitry Peskov said Friday that the peace track is on a "deep pause" and that there are "no new proposals whatsoever," while Russian forces press Pokrovsk and Kupiansk and, in his telling, make gains. Twenty-four hours earlier the CIA director's first known Moscow trip was the reason we raised the ceasefire number three points. The Kremlin has now answered that channel in public, and the caveat we attached at the time - that Peskov kept the contact deliberately at agency level with no Putin meeting - did all the work. A belligerent that believes it is winning does not settle; the bargaining model of war says fighting continues precisely while both sides' expectations diverge, and Russia has just told us where its expectations sit.

brief.h: Iran offers a hand, Washington promises a fist, on the same day
brief.t: Abbas Araghchi met Qatar's foreign minister and called diplomacy "not impossible," then set the price again: the US should build trust, speak respectfully, acknowledge Iran's rights and uphold its commitments - the eighth restatement of the condition stack since February. Hours later Treasury Secretary Bessent said Operation Economic Outcast would crush Iran's economy and took the campaign into the G20 finance track. Schelling's rule is that compellence works only when the climb-down is made cheap; Washington raised the price of Tehran's concession on the day Tehran gestured at making one. Transits through the strait fell back below their ten-day average.

brief.h: The market has already priced the post-summit thaw
brief.t: Polymarket puts a US announcement ending the Iranian blockade at 69% by December 31 but only 24% by September 30 and 4% by September 7 - roughly $330k of 24-hour volume across the family. The crowd is not forecasting a breakthrough; it is forecasting a calendar, with almost all the probability mass landing after the September 24 Xi summit. That is independent confirmation of the reading that Washington is holding the Hormuz file as leverage through Beijing, and it is why our post-summit-concession forecast moved six points today. Note the contrast: the same book prices the strait itself returning to normal by September 30 at 4%. The market expects the US to lift its blockade well before Iran lifts its toll.

brief.h: The carrier headline is a sustainment story, not an escalation
brief.t: The Theodore Roosevelt sails from San Diego in coming weeks for a deployment of more than seven months, relieving the George Washington, which itself relieved the Abraham Lincoln - a ship that spent over 250 days at sea without a port call amid reported supply shortages, a sailor overboard and at least one suicide attempt. Read as a primary indicator rather than a headline, that is force generation being consumed by presence. Continuous carrier coverage of one theatre is the readiness cost of a standoff, and it is evidence against, not for, the capacity to open a new multi-day campaign. Our strike-resumption number came down two points on it.

brief.h: Underneath the maritime file, the nuclear one is still frozen
brief.t: Iran's nuclear chief said the bombed sites remain uncleared for inspection because of the wartime situation, and the agency has still not regained access to the Esfahan enrichment plant declared just before the war. Highly enriched uranium under a comprehensive safeguards agreement is supposed to be verified every thirty days; that clock has been broken for months. Everyone is negotiating over a waterway, but the thing that started the war is unmonitored, and any Hormuz arrangement that leaves the inspection question untouched buys shipping lanes without buying stability.

lesson: When Peskov said the peace track was on a deep pause, the instinctive reading is that the war just got longer. Korea says otherwise. Truce talks opened at Kaesong on 10 July 1951, thirteen months into the war, and the armistice was not signed at Panmunjom until 27 July 1953 - two years and seventeen days in which the negotiators met, walked out, sat in silence for weeks at a time, and met again while the front barely moved. Close to half of all American casualties in that war were suffered after the talking began. The two lessons are uncomfortable and both apply now. First, talks and fighting are not alternatives but the same process: a pause in negotiation is a bargaining move inside the negotiation, not its end, and Pokrovsk is where Russia is making its argument this week. Second, the final obstacle is usually not the map - Korea's front line was settled by November 1951 and the remaining twenty months were spent arguing about prisoner repatriation, a question nobody had listed as central. So when this war does move, expect the sticking point to be something not currently on anyone's agenda: not Donbas, but the guarantees, the elections, or who verifies what.

lecture.title: The Toll Collector, the Prince, and the End of the Interlude

sections.t: Iran's permit regime feels unprecedented; it isn't. Denmark ran the Sound Dues from 1429 to 1857 — every ship entering the Baltic paid the crown at Elsinore, financing the Danish state for four centuries, until the maritime nations bought the strait free by treaty. The double lesson: a chokepoint toll is durable when the collector is strong and the fee bearable, fatal when the collector is weak and patience runs out. Nasser survived nationalizing Suez in 1956 because the superpowers split; Egypt closed Tiran in 1967 and had war inside three weeks. Iran's PGSA is trying to be Denmark; its kinetic enforcement keeps veering toward Tiran. And today's US convoy escorts rerun Operation Earnest Will (1987–8), which ended with the US Navy destroying half of Iran's fleet in a day after a single mine strike. Both governments know this history — which is why the standoff is so combustible.

The Islamic Republic's founding claim — guardianship of the jurist — was a rejection of dynasty; 1979 overthrew a hereditary monarch. Mojtaba's eight-day accession, over his father's written objection to family succession and under documented Revolutionary Guard pressure, quietly converted the republic into the thing it was born to destroy: a monarchy guarded by praetorians. Praetorian institutions — Rome's Guard, the Ottoman Janissaries, Pakistan's army economy — convert national crisis into institutional power; the emergency is the business model. An IRGC collecting two-million-dollar tolls in bitcoin while the national export terminal sits idle is not irrational. It is the type behaving as the type always has. That is why a managed, toll-preserving reopening is far likelier than a free strait: institutions do not dissolve themselves.

Russia has no natural western frontier — the North European Plain runs flat from the Urals to the Atlantic — and every Russian state since Muscovy has answered that geography by pushing the buffer outward. This is the latest partition war over the borderlands, settled into attrition, and attrition wars end through exhaustion, usually via armistice: Korea 1953 is the governing template. The obstacle is the credible-commitment problem, and Ukraine is its textbook victim — in 1994 it surrendered the world's third-largest nuclear arsenal for the Budapest Memorandum's paper assurances, from, among others, Russia. Every guarantee now on offer is negotiated in the shadow of that betrayal.

Beijing's current quiet should be read through 1914, not 1938. The dangerous moments come from window logic — Germany went to war partly because its generals believed Russia would be unbeatable by 1917. China's demographics have peaked and US munitions are visibly depleted; a closing-window calculation could form within a decade. Against it: nuclear deterrence, the hardest amphibious operation in warfare, and fabs worth more unburnt. The coast-guard creep east of Taiwan is Schelling's salami tactics — each slice too thin to fight over. Gray-zone strategies fail only when they force the defender to a bright line; whether the slicing continues through the September summit is this month's test of which game Beijing is playing.

What you are watching is the closing of the unipolar interlude — the thirty years when one navy underwrote every strait and major-power war was priced near zero. It is ending the way Britain's underwriting ended between 1914 and 1947: piecemeal, strait by strait, with the old hegemon monetizing what it once provided free — note Washington now charging for convoy protection — and middle powers suddenly indispensable: Pakistan mediating, Oman hosting, the Gulf selling to both blocs. The nineteenth century would recognize this world instantly. The twentieth would not.

Four structural calls. This is probably the last great oil-chokepoint crisis — 2026 is doing to electrification what 1973 did to the IEA and North Sea oil; by the 2040s Hormuz matters like coaling stations did in 1950 (moderate-high confidence). The proliferation dam is cracked: Ukraine disarmed and was invaded, Iran lacked the bomb and was decapitated, North Korea is untouched — expect one to three new nuclear or threshold states in twenty years, the worst trend on the board (moderate). Russia's trajectory is Ottoman: declining, dangerous because declining, ending as junior partner to the neighbor it once dominated (high confidence on direction, none on timing). And the hinge of the century is whether a democracy keeps paying hegemony's domestic costs — decided less in Taiwan than in Washington's budgets and gas prices (genuinely uncertain). Reading: Kennedy's Rise and Fall of the Great Powers; Schelling's Arms and Influence; Yergin's The Prize; Kotkin on Russia.
